# Powwow Lang — LLM reference

This is a complete, self-contained reference for Powwow, a small embeddable templating language for .NET. It is intended to be loaded as context so you can read and write Powwow templates correctly. Human-facing docs: README.md, docs/overview.md, docs/datatypes.md, docs/directives.md, docs/functions.md, grammar.md.

## What Powwow is

Powwow renders data-driven text (originally HTML email templates). A template is plain text with `{{ ... }}` directives embedded in it. Text outside directives is emitted verbatim; directives are evaluated. The interpreter is written in dependency-free .NET Framework and embeds into host apps, which supply data, custom functions, and template resolution. The host calls `interpreter.Interpret(templateString, dataObject)` and gets back a rendered string.

Influences: JavaScript (expressions, lambdas, objects), Handlebars/Liquid (directives, whitespace control). Objects are prototype-less. There is no `null` type.

## Directives

- `{{ expr }}` — evaluate an expression and emit its result. E.g. `{{ user.name }}`, `{{ 2 + 3 }}`, `{{ toUpper(s) }}`.
- Whitespace inside a directive is insignificant: `{{x}}` == `{{ x }}`.
- Keyword directives: `let`, `mut`, `if`/`elseif`/`else`/`/if`, `for`/`/for`, `capture`/`/capture`, `include`, `literal`/`/literal`, and comments.

### Whitespace control

Whitespace and newlines around a directive are part of the output. Add a hyphen to a delimiter to trim:
- `{{-` trims whitespace and the single newline IMMEDIATELY BEFORE the directive.
- `-}}` trims whitespace and the single newline IMMEDIATELY AFTER the directive.
- Each marker trims only one adjacent newline (plus spaces/tabs on that side), not a whole run of blank lines.
- Use these to keep output clean, especially around `let`/`for`/`if` lines that emit nothing themselves.

Example:
```
{{- let name = "Ada" -}}
Hello, {{ name }}!
```
Output: `Hello, Ada!`

### Comments

`{{* ... *}}` — never evaluated, emits nothing. May span lines and contain `{{`/`}}`. Hyphens allowed: `{{-* ... *-}}`.

### Literal blocks

`{{ literal }} ... {{ /literal }}` — emits the body verbatim; directives inside are NOT interpreted. May be nested.

## Variables: let / assignment

- `{{ let x = expr }}` declares and binds a new variable.
- `{{ x = expr }}` reassigns an EXISTING variable.
- `{{ obj.field = expr }}` updates an EXISTING field of an object (dot notation, one level).
- Assignment does NOT create new variables or add new object fields — only `let` (variables) and `obj(...)` (fields) do.
- The `mut` keyword is OPTIONAL and DEPRECATED: `{{ mut x = expr }}` is identical to `{{ x = expr }}`. It still works (and existing templates keep running) but may be REMOVED in a future version — do not use `mut` in new templates; prefer plain assignment. The same applies inside lambda statement lists (`(() => let x = 1, x = 2, x)()`).

## Conditionals: if

```
{{ if cond }} ... {{ elseif cond2 }} ... {{ else }} ... {{ /if }}
```
The condition must be a boolean expression. `elseif`/`else` are optional. There is also a functional inline form: the `if(cond, then, else)` built-in (returns a value; both branches lazy). Each branch is BLOCK-SCOPED: a `let` inside a branch does not leak out (see Scoping).

## Loops: for

```
{{ for item in arrayExpr }} ... {{ /for }}
```
Iterates an array, binding each element to the loop variable. Pairs with `range(...)` and the `rangeX(...)` date functions.

## Capture

```
{{ capture name }} ...body... {{ /capture }}
```
Evaluates the body, stores the RENDERED STRING into a new variable `name`, and emits nothing at the site. Body may contain any directives (loops, if, include). The body is BLOCK-SCOPED: only `name` is published to the surrounding scope; `let`s used inside the body are local to it (see Scoping).

## Composition: include

`{{ include templateName }}` renders another template inline by bare name. Requires the host to supply an `ITemplateResolver`; otherwise unavailable. Included templates are BLOCK-SCOPED: they run in their own scope and can read the names in scope at the include site plus host data and functions, but their top-level `let`s do NOT leak back to the caller — an include publishes nothing back, only rendered text (see Scoping). Circular includes are detected and error.

## Scoping

Lexical scoping. A NEW scope is created by: a lambda call, each `for` iteration, each `if`/`elseif`/`else` branch, each `capture` body, and each `include` (the included template runs in its own scope). The root template body is the global scope (host data + registered functions).

- A `let` inside a scope is LOCAL and discarded when the block ends — it does NOT leak out. So a `let` declared in an `if`/`capture`/`for` body is invisible afterward (`Unknown identifier`).
- NO SHADOWING: an inner `let` may not reuse a name visible in an enclosing scope (it errors, it does not shadow). Exception: lambda parameters may reuse an outer name and take precedence inside the lambda.
- Reassigning an OUTER variable from inside a scope (`x = ...`) reaches the outer binding and persists after the block.
- A `capture` publishes only its variable to the enclosing scope; an `include` publishes nothing back (it emits rendered text only).
- Resolution order: current scope -> enclosing scopes (for a lambda: its definition/closure scope, then the caller) -> global data -> registered functions. Unresolved name errors.
- IMMUTABLE (reassignment errors): loop variables, lambda parameters, host/global data, registered functions. MUTABLE: `let` variables and the fields of objects they hold.
- No "declare without value". To set a variable conditionally: declare it with a default first, then reassign inside the branch — `{{ let x = "Free" }}{{ if cond }}{{ x = "Premium" }}{{ /if }}` — or use the expression form `{{ let x = if(cond, "Premium", "Free") }}`, or `capture`.

## Data types

Powwow has 7 types. Check a value's type with `typeof(v)` compared to a type literal: `Number`, `String`, `Boolean`, `Array`, `Object`, `Function`, `DateTime`.

- **Number** — floating point (decimal); no separate int type. Literals: `42`, `-2.5`, `.6`, `0.7`. Operators `+ - * /` with parentheses and standard precedence. Note: decimal SCALE propagates, so `2.5 + 1.5` renders `4.0` and integer division like `10 / 4` renders `2.5`; results that stay integer-scaled render without a decimal point.
- **String** — double-quoted, Unicode OK: `"Hello 😀"`. Escapes: `\"` `\\` `\n` `\r` `\t`. No unicode escapes. Equality with `==`/`!=`.
- **Boolean** — `true` / `false`. Operators `&&` `||` `!` (short-circuit). Equality `==`/`!=`. No ordering (`< <= > >=` are numbers-only).
- **Array** — `[expr, expr, ...]`, mixed types allowed, may nest: `[1, "two", false, [4,5]]`. REFERENCE TYPE: `==` is identity, not element-wise; assignment shares the same underlying array. Index with subscript syntax `arr[i]` or the equivalent `at(arr, i)` function; `i` must be a whole number (fractional/negative/out-of-bounds errors). Subscripts chain: `arr[0][1]`.
- **Object** — `obj(key: expr, ...)` with bare (unquoted) identifier keys, prototype-less. Read fields with dot notation `o.field` (errors if absent — guard with `contains`), with string subscript `o["field"]`, or `get(o, "field")` for computed keys. REFERENCE TYPE like arrays. Functions can be fields and called via dot: `o.fn(x)`.
- **DateTime** — no literal; produced by `datetime("...")`, `now()`, `utcNow()`. Renders ISO 8601 by default; `format(d, fmt)` for .NET format strings. Equality is by instant.
- **Function** — lambdas and built-ins are first-class values; `typeof(lambda) == Function`.

## Operators and precedence

Lowest to highest: `||`, then `&&`, then comparison (`< <= > >= == !=`), then `+ -`, then `* /`, then unary `!`, then primary. Group with `( )`. Comparisons and arithmetic are infix; ordering operators apply to numbers only; `==`/`!=` work on all types (reference identity for arrays/objects).

## Lambdas, functions, closures

- Lambda: `(a, b) => expr`. Zero args: `() => expr`. Optional local statements before the result: `(x) => let y = x * 2, y + 1`.
- First-class: pass lambdas to `map`/`filter`/`reduce`/`order`, store in variables or object fields.
- Closures capture surrounding variables. Recursion is supported (host sets a max recursion depth, default 1000).
- Built-ins are overloaded by argument type; passing an unsupported type errors.

## Built-in functions

Signatures below; `arg = default` marks optional trailing args. Built-ins never mutate arguments and return new values. Failures (bad index, missing field, unparseable string) raise errors rather than returning null.

Type/convert:
- `typeof(value)` -> type literal
- `string(number|boolean)` -> String  ("true"/"false" for booleans)
- `number(string)` -> Number (errors if not numeric)
- `numeric(string)` -> Boolean (parseable?)

Numbers:
- `range(start, end, step = 1)` -> Array of Number; end EXCLUSIVE; step may be negative, not zero
- `mod(a, b)` -> Number (integer remainder; b != 0)
- `floor(n)`, `ceil(n)` -> Number
- `round(n, decimals = 0)` -> Number

Strings:
- `length(s)` -> Number
- `empty(s)` -> Boolean
- `concat(a, b)` -> String
- `contains(s, search)`, `startsWith(s, search)`, `endsWith(s, search)` -> Boolean
- `indexOf(s, search)`, `lastIndexOf(s, search)` -> Number (-1 if absent)
- `substring(s, start, end = -1)` -> String (start inclusive, end exclusive; to end if omitted)
- `toUpper(s)`, `toLower(s)`, `trim(s)` -> String
- `explode(s, delimiter)` -> Array (inverse of join)

Arrays:
- `length(xs)` -> Number
- `at(xs, index)` -> element (0-based; out-of-bounds errors). Equivalent to subscript syntax `xs[index]`.
- `first(xs)`, `last(xs)` -> element (error if empty); `rest(xs)` -> Array (all but first)
- `any(xs)` -> Boolean (non-empty?)
- `concat(a, b)` -> Array
- `take(xs, n)`, `skip(xs, n)` -> Array
- `map(xs, (x) => ...)` -> Array
- `filter(xs, (x) => boolean)` -> Array
- `reduce(xs, (acc, x) => ..., initial)` -> value
- `order(xs)` | `order(xs, ascendingBool)` | `order(xs, (a, b) => number)` -> Array (sorted copy)
- `group(xs, fieldName)` -> Object keyed by that string field; values are arrays
- `join(xs, delimiter)` -> String

Objects:
- `get(obj, key)` -> value (errors if missing)
- `contains(obj, key)` -> Boolean
- `keys(obj)` -> Array of String

DateTime:
- `datetime(s)` -> DateTime (parse; errors if invalid)
- `now()`, `utcNow()` -> DateTime
- `format(d, fmtString)` -> String (.NET format)
- `addYears(d, n)`, `addMonths`, `addDays`, `addHours`, `addMinutes`, `addSeconds` -> new DateTime (n may be negative)
- `rangeYear(start, end, step = 1)`, `rangeMonth`, `rangeDay`, `rangeHour`, `rangeMinute`, `rangeSecond` -> Array of DateTime; end EXCLUSIVE; step positive

JSON:
- `fromJson(s)` -> value (objects/arrays/primitives)
- `toJson(value, formatted = false)` -> String

Web/encoding:
- `htmlEncode(s)`, `htmlDecode(s)`, `urlEncode(s)`, `urlDecode(s)` -> String
- `uri(s)` -> Object with URL parts: Scheme, Host, Port, AbsolutePath, PathAndQuery, Query, Fragment, Segments (Array), plus booleans like IsAbsoluteUri, IsFile, IsLoopback

Control flow:
- `if(cond, then, else)` -> value (both branches evaluated lazily)

Dataverse (only if host supplies a Dataverse service):
- `fetch(fetchXml)` -> query results

## Common pitfalls (read before writing templates)

1. Subscripts are type-specific: array subscripts need a whole-number index (`arr[0]`), object subscripts need a string key (`obj["k"]`). `arr["0"]` or `obj[0]` errors. `at(arr, i)` and `get(obj, "k")` are the function equivalents.
2. Accessing a missing object field ERRORS. Guard with `contains(obj, "field")` first.
3. Assignment (`x = ...`, or the optional legacy `mut x = ...`) only reassigns existing variables/fields; it cannot add a new field to an object or declare a new variable.
4. Arrays and objects are reference types: `==` compares identity, not contents; copying a variable shares the same value (mutations are visible through both names).
5. Strings that look like dates are still strings; convert with `datetime(...)` before using date functions.
6. Booleans don't support `< <= > >=` (numbers only).
7. There is no `null`. Functions error instead of returning null/empty.
8. Decimal scale shows through: division and decimal literals can render trailing decimals (e.g. `4.0`). Use `round(x, n)` to control display.
9. Whitespace around no-output directives (`let`, `for`, `if`) stays in the output unless you use `{{-`/`-}}`.
10. `range`/`rangeX` ends are EXCLUSIVE.
11. `if`/`elseif`/`else` branches, `capture` bodies, and included templates are BLOCK-SCOPED: a `let` inside does not survive the block (for an include, does not leak back to the caller), and cannot shadow an outer name. To compute a value conditionally, declare it with a default before the block and reassign inside (`{{ let x = "Free" }}{{ if c }}{{ x = "Premium" }}{{ /if }}`), or use `{{ let x = if(c, a, b) }}`. Reassigning an outer variable from inside a block does persist.

## Worked examples

Greeting with inline conditional:
```
{{- let user = obj(name: "Ada", premium: true) -}}
Hi {{ user.name }}, {{ if(user.premium, "thanks for being premium!", "enjoy your free account!") }}
```
-> `Hi Ada, thanks for being premium!`

List with a loop and trimming:
```
{{- let xs = ["red", "green", "blue"] -}}
{{- for x in xs -}}
- {{ x }}
{{ /for -}}
```
->
```
- red
- green
- blue
```

Transform a collection:
```
{{- let nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] -}}
{{ map(nums, (x) => x * x) }}
{{ filter(nums, (x) => x > 2) }}
{{ reduce(nums, (acc, x) => acc + x, 0) }}
```
->
```
[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
[3, 4, 5]
15
```

Objects and safe field access:
```
{{- let user = obj(name: "Ada", age: 36) -}}
{{ user.name }} is {{ user.age }}
{{ if contains(user, "email") }}{{ user.email }}{{ else }}no email on file{{ /if }}
```
->
```
Ada is 36
no email on file
```

Dates:
```
{{- let d = datetime("2024-01-08 10:10:10") -}}
{{ format(d, "yyyy-MM-dd") }}
{{ format(addDays(d, 30), "MMM d, yyyy") }}
```
->
```
2024-01-08
Feb 7, 2024
```
